name: Elastin peptides

card.summary: Fragments of the skin protein elastin, used in cosmetic creams and supplements to support the springy, firm look of skin.

quick.overview:
Elastin is the protein in the skin's elastic fibres that lets skin spring back after being pinched or stretched. Elastin peptides are broken-down fragments of it, and cosmetic products use similar fragments hoping to support skin firmness.
The appearance goal is firmer, more elastic-looking skin as elastic fibres thin and fragment with age. Research on elastin peptides is mostly laboratory biology, in which they act as signalling fragments.
quick.how: They appear as ingredients in creams and serums and in oral supplements. People apply or take them alongside other skin routines such as sunscreen and retinoids.
quick.risks: No major safety signals for cosmetic use have been reported. In biology, elastin fragments are studied for roles in disease processes such as tumour progression.

lead: Elastin forms the dermal elastic fibres, combined with fibrillin, which let skin return to its original position when pinched [1]. Elastin is extremely long-lived (half-life over 78 years), yet fewer, more fragmented elastic fibres are seen in ageing skin, linked to reduced firmness especially in sun-exposed areas [1].

Elastin peptides are the degradation products of elastin. Biology reviews describe them as matrikines, fragments of matrix proteins with biological activity, which attract several cell types, promote cell cycle progression and trigger release of proteolytic enzymes [2]. Cosmetic products offer elastin or elastin-like peptides on the idea that these fragments or building blocks support skin structure.

Controlled evidence for topical or oral elastin peptides improving visible skin appearance was not found; related research on recombinant tropoelastin in wounds produced new elastin fibres without significantly improving scar appearance [1].

chain: Elastin fragments supplied in a cream or supplement
Claimed support for dermal elastic fibres
angle.text: Products position elastin peptides as a way to counter the loss of skin spring with age. The claimed route is support for elastic fibres, and its effect on appearance in humans has not been established in controlled trials found.

paras: Tropoelastin, elastin's soluble precursor of about 50 to 70 kDa, aggregates at body temperature and is cross-linked by the copper-dependent enzyme lysyl oxidase into insoluble mature elastin [1]. Sun exposure can cause excess elastin accumulation known as actinic elastosis [1].
Elastin peptides bind to an elastin-laminin receptor and signal to cells; the term elastokine describes matrikines from elastin fragmentation, and some peptides mimic their effects [2].

No studies found on cosmetic elastin peptides. Wikipedia notes that an uncontrolled five-person study of an amino-acid-copper skin booster saw measured elasticity rise 23.4%, with larger controlled studies needed [1].
